Pet Rent, Pet Deposit, and Pet Fee: What Renters Really Pay

Understand how pet rent, pet deposits, and pet fees differ, which ones you get back, and how to total the real yearly cost of renting with a dog.

Published: 2026-10-03Sources checked: 2Educational planning guide

A pet deposit is usually refundable, a pet fee is a one-time charge you do not get back, and pet rent is a recurring monthly charge added to your base rent. Knowing which is which tells you what a lease with a dog actually costs over a year.

Three charges that sound alike but behave differently

Landlords use three separate charges for renters with pets, and they are not interchangeable. According to a landlord guide from Landlord Studio, a pet deposit is refundable and works like a security deposit earmarked for pet-related damage, a pet fee is a one-time non-refundable charge, and pet rent is a recurring monthly charge added to your rent.

  • Pet deposit: held against damage; returned after move-out if the unit is undamaged beyond normal wear.
  • Pet fee: paid once at move-in and kept regardless of whether your dog causes any damage.
  • Pet rent: billed every month for the life of the lease and never returned.

The same source explains why the labels exist. A pet fee is meant to offset general turnover costs a pet can add, such as deep-cleaning carpets or repainting to remove odors. Pet rent, by contrast, is treated as part of monthly rent, which is why the Landlord Studio guide notes it is legal in most states to charge both pet rent and a pet deposit at the same time. A DoorLoop guide frames the same trio similarly, describing pet rent as a recurring monthly add-on, a pet deposit as a one-time refundable amount for damage, and a pet fee as a one-time non-refundable charge for wear and tear.

Both sources stress that whether a deposit must be kept separate from the standard security deposit, and how large the total may be, differs by state law. Read the lease label carefully, because the word used decides whether you ever see that money again.

Why the word on the lease decides your refund

The Landlord Studio guide stresses that a charge labeled a deposit cannot quietly become non-refundable later, and that most states require explicit written disclosure of which charges are refundable. It lists what your lease should spell out: the exact amount of each charge, which charges are refundable and which are not, what a refundable deposit can be used for, and the timeline and process for returning it. That means the safest thing you can do is read the pet addendum before you sign and confirm, in writing, which dollars come back.

Refundable deposits also reward good behavior: the same guide explains that a pet deposit should only be used for damage beyond normal wear, not routine cleaning or minor scuffs. It recommends that landlords document the unit's condition with photos at move-in and again at move-out, and provide itemized deductions with receipts. As a renter, you can do the same on your side, photographing the unit at move-in so you have your own record if there is a dispute later. For a broader look at how housing rules shape your options, see our guide to apartment lease restrictions for dog owners.

How state deposit caps can affect you

One reason buildings lean on non-refundable fees is that many states cap the total security deposit a landlord may hold, often at one or two months' rent. The Landlord Studio guide points out that if a landlord is already collecting a full security deposit, adding a large pet deposit could push the total past the state limit, so some landlords use a higher non-refundable pet fee instead, because fees are generally not subject to deposit caps.

For you as a renter, this has a practical effect: a building in a strict-cap state may quote you a non-refundable fee where another building would take a refundable deposit. That is not necessarily a worse deal, but it changes how much of your money is recoverable. When you compare two buildings, separate the refundable dollars from the non-refundable ones rather than comparing a single lump sum. The DoorLoop guide similarly advises confirming your state's rules before assuming a charge is allowed or refundable.

A worksheet to total your real yearly cost

Instead of guessing, fill this worksheet with the exact numbers your prospective building quotes you. Amounts vary widely by city and property, so use your own lease figures rather than averages. Work through it once per building you are seriously considering, so you can compare true totals side by side.

LineFormulaYour number
One-time pet feefee per pet x number of pets____
Refundable pet depositdeposit amount (recorded, not spent)____
Annual pet rentmonthly pet rent x 12____
Pet rent over the leasemonthly pet rent x lease months____
First-year out-of-pocketpet fee + annual pet rent____
Deposit at riskdeposit you could lose to damage____

The first-year out-of-pocket line is the number most renters underestimate, because monthly pet rent quietly adds up over twelve months, and the lease-length line shows the full commitment if you renew. Treat the deposit separately: it is money parked, not money spent, unless your dog causes damage, and in most cases you should get it back. Keep the refundable and non-refundable columns visually distinct so a building with a big refundable deposit is not confused with one that keeps the same amount as a fee. Combine this with our five-year ownership cost framework to see how housing charges stack against food, vet care, and grooming across the years you will own your dog.

A realistic lease-signing walkthrough

Picture touring a building you like. The agent mentions pet costs in passing. Here is how to turn that into clear numbers before you commit:

  1. Ask for each charge by name and get the amount for your specific dog and unit.
  2. Ask which charges are refundable and request that answer in the written pet addendum.
  3. Multiply the monthly pet rent by your lease length so you see the full commitment, not the monthly sticker.
  4. Photograph and note existing wear at move-in, especially floors, doors, and baseboards.
  5. Confirm the move-out inspection process and the timeline for returning your deposit.

If the building will not put the refundable-versus-non-refundable breakdown in writing, treat that as a warning sign and keep looking.

Assistance animals are treated differently

Service animals and assistance animals are not treated as pets under the federal Fair Housing Act, so the usual pet charges do not all apply. A DoorLoop landlord guide, citing the Humane Society's summary of the Fair Housing Act and assistance animals, explains that owners do not have to pay pet fees for these animals, but a landlord can still charge a security deposit and may seek money for any damage the animal causes to the home.

This is a legal area with details that vary, so if you rely on an assistance animal, confirm your specific situation with the housing provider and, if needed, a qualified professional rather than assuming a blanket rule applies to you.

Mistakes renters make with pet charges

  • Reading only the monthly number. Pet rent looks small per month but is the largest line over a full lease.
  • Assuming a deposit is refundable because it is called a deposit. Get refundability in writing.
  • Skipping move-in photos. Without them, you cannot dispute damage deductions later.
  • Forgetting per-pet math. Two dogs can mean two of every charge.
  • Not budgeting for the deposit at all. Even refundable money has to be available up front.

What this guide cannot tell you

This guide cannot quote the exact fees your city, building, or landlord will charge, because those numbers vary by market and change over time. It also cannot give you legal advice about your lease or your rights as a tenant with an assistance animal. State and local laws set caps and disclosure rules that differ from place to place. Use the worksheet with real quotes from real buildings, read your pet addendum closely, and consult a local housing resource or attorney for questions about your specific rights.

FAQ

Is a pet deposit the same as a pet fee?
No. According to the Landlord Studio guide, a pet deposit is refundable and set aside for pet-related damage, while a pet fee is a one-time charge you do not get back. The label on your lease matters, so confirm in writing which charges are refundable before you sign, and photograph the unit at move-in to protect your deposit.
Can a landlord charge pet rent and a pet deposit at the same time?
In most states, yes, because they serve different purposes: pet rent is treated as part of monthly rent and a pet deposit works as security. The Landlord Studio guide notes that total deposits may still be capped by state law, so a large pet deposit could bump you over local limits. Always verify your state and local rules.
Do I pay pet fees for a service or support animal?
Not pet fees. A DoorLoop landlord guide, citing the Humane Society's summary of the Fair Housing Act, explains that service and assistance animals are not treated as pets, so owners do not pay pet fees. The landlord can, however, charge a security deposit and may seek money for damage the animal causes. Confirm your specific situation with the housing provider or a qualified professional.
